In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new type of column system, the multi-column system, which can cover a wide range of column efficiencies in a single analysis, and which can thus be used to realize ultra-high speed and ultra-high resolution separations in a single analysis.
the development of new concepts for the design of multi-column systems that are able to cover a wide range of plate numbers with a minimal loss of analysis time.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a multi-column system should always be built in a serially-connected mode.
the serial connection variant should be preferred for multi-column systems, but that the parallel connection variant should be used for the highest efficiency columns (e.g. 75,000 plates or above).
the serial connection is the best way to realize a multi-column system covering a wide range of column efficiencies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the serial connection variant is the best compromise between analysis time and amount of required column material for a multi-column system spanning a wide range in column length, and thus efficiency, and that this variant should be preferred over parallel connection for all applications where a wide-efficiency range is needed, including UHPLC applications.

the serial connection of columns is the better approach for the construction of wide range systems, while the parallel connection of columns is a better approach for covering a narrower range of efficiencies.

a multi-column system with individually optimized column segments should be able to get very close to the Knox & Saleemspeed limit, and should be a very useful tool to improve the speed of analysis of samples with very wide peak widths.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the serial connection of columns with different lengths offers the best compromise between speed and amount of silica required to cover a wide range of column efficiencies.

the serial connection is the better approach when aiming at the highest possible speed and the lowest required amount of silica for a given dynamic range of efficiency, whereas the parallel approach is the better choice for a given amount of required silica and when aiming at a high dynamic range of efficiency.

the construction of systems covering wide ranges of efficiencies is best done by using serially connected segments, and that the best possible compromise between speed and amount of silica is obtained when the segments are individually tuned for their optimum length.
